newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs will have to work with former foes - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Serbs will have to work with former foes - diplomats.

text.p: Despite fiery separatist rhetoric during the election campaign, Bosnian Serb hardliners accept they will have to cooperate with their wartime foes and take part in Bosnia's new inter-communal government, Western diplomats said on Tuesday.

The separatist SDS party which led the Bosnian Serb war effort was poised to overwhelm "moderates" in the battle for the Serb seat on the new collective Bosnian presidency and for control of a Bosnian Serb assembly.
A partial count of the returns in Saturday's vote showed that SDS candidate Momcilo Krajisnik was certain to join the three-man Bosnian presidency.
All three sides used tough talk on the stump but diplomats believe that was mostly posturing.
Krajisnik is the most powerful politician in the Bosnian Serb republic and the fact that he was nominated was a sure sign that that thew SDS was taking the presidency seriously, diplomats said.
"Krajisnik would have not stood for something that has no influence," one added.

Although the election results appeared to be confirming the ascendancy of hardliners on all sides, some analysts believe elections mean that Bosnia has taken a stride to peace that will be irreversible under strict scrutiny by the international community.
The presidency members are expected to be invited to the United Nations next month where "each will have to commit himself to Bosnia in the eyes of the entire world," the diplomatic source said.
"The Bosnian Serbs have so far been living in a limbo. Now they have a state and their leaders will have to play by international rules or else."

The first to swallow the bitter pill of international pressure in that respect was Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who was forced by mediators at the weekend to to retract her separatist statements.

"In 1990 (Bosnian Serb leader Radovan) Karadzic promised his Moslem and Croat rivals in the parliament the the gates of hell would soon open. We have now shut them formally and we will have no more such rhetoric," the diplomat said.
Senior Bosnian Serb sources close to the government acknowledge that Serbs have no option but to cooperate.
"Even as we speak the authorities are looking for 40 ambassadors," he said.

The Dayton peace accord has divided Bosnia into a Moslem-Croat federation and a Bosnian Serb republic joined in a loose decentralised state. Each of the ethnic groups wil have its share of ambassadorial posts which will represent the new Bosnia in the world.

"How do you then advocate only national interests. It's impossible. How do you play up nationalist obstruction when the entire world, including your own people see you on television sitting together with Moslems and Croats," the Bosnian Serb source said.
Diplomats said the Bosnian Serb leaders have played straight into the hands of Serbian President Slobodan MIlosevic who wants to distance himself from Bosnia as much and as quickly as possible.

Cut off from mother Serbia, the Bosnian Serb republic will have to turn to the world for financial assistance and rely on reviving its industry which was built to depend on other parts of Bosnia for energy, raw materials and markets.

"If the SDS does not rapidly improve the standard of living of its voters while back pedalling on its war goals, allowing refugees to return and extraditing war criminals, it will face political death at the next elections," the diplomat said.
"There is no way of getting out of this. Once the ball starts rolling all the nationalist leaders will have to choke on the reasons for starting this war and start cooperating," he added.
